title: Which Quotes Should You Learn?
author: Dominic Salles
summary: A GCSE student asks Dominic Salles whether 18 Macbeth quotes with analysis, generated by Claude, are any good. Salles answers by first tackling the larger question of whether to use AI at all, quoting a YouTube commenter who called him a hypocrite and explaining his own rule: do not let AI do your thinking, but do let it do work you would otherwise pay someone to do. He gives an honest example of an AI-animated video that students watched for less time, so he will not make more. The main lesson is that quotes are useless until you test yourself: study the quotes and analysis, put them aside, write them from memory, and use AI to quiz you with progressively harder gap-fill exercises. He then recommends practicing essays by speaking them aloud with dictation, and suggests spacing practice across texts to build memory. He ends with the AI-generated quote set, grouped by theme with alternative-view quotes, and his own view that the academic language is more advanced than students need.
points: Salles's rule for AI is to think first, then use AI to challenge your thinking, and delegate only tasks you would otherwise pay for.
AI-generated quotes and analysis are useless until the student has tested themselves and learned them.
Progressive gap-fill quizzes, from first letters to blanks to recall from the prompt, make quotes and analysis stick.
Speaking a practice essay with voice dictation lets a student rehearse about four questions an hour and see how well the quotes fit.
Spacing practice across different texts forces recall and builds stronger memory than cramming one text.
quotes: So, get AI to test your thinking. Get AI to tell you what to go and find out next. Get AI to ask you questions and challenge your answers. If AI makes you think, you will learn much more than a person not using AI.

So, now I design a thumbnail myself, and I also get AI to make two alternative versions. YouTube tests all 3, sending each one at random to different viewers. I then select the one that gets the most views. Annoyingly this is often the AI thumbnail. It just works.
No, it has not worked. Students don’t like the thumbnail. Even when they click (knowing it is AI from the thumbnail), they watch the video for less time.
This is the right thought. But when you get the quotes, it is of little use, because you can’t use it yet. You haven’t thought about the quote itself, or the analysis of it.
The ‘so what’ is that you have to apply it to different questions, and see if the quotes fit. See if you understand the analysis.
Study the quotes and the analysis. Then put them aside. Write a list of the quotes from memory. Keep testing yourself until you know them.

You can fully revise 4 questions per hour of revision if you are smashing it. You will learn more if you do only one hour a week with different texts, because this will force you to remember the quotes and analysis. When you leave gaps, you build stronger memory - that’s just the science.
Personally, I don’t like the academic language, I think it is much more advanced than you need, and the more words you don’t understand, the harder it is to learn.
